title: The School Year Is a Long Walk
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien argues that a principal is a 'Chief Systems Officer' whose job runs on three verbs — design, implement, monitor — and that the strategic plan is only the first, easiest third. He recounts turning one school year into a literal 'walk across the country,' borrowing Collins and Hansen's '20 Mile March': 172 instructional days at twenty miles a day covers the roughly 3,400 miles from Los Angeles to the coast of Maine, and each Monday's staff email reported the miles walked, the state reached, and the landmarks passed. The point of the metaphor was honesty — a monitoring instrument disguised as a story that kept the strategic plan alive past the February point where most plans quietly die. But O'Brien's deeper claim is that almost all school leadership is change management wearing other names: the map does not walk, the plan does not walk, people walk. Teachers are an unforgiving audience because they carry the accumulated weight of poorly executed past initiatives, so the leader's real work is winning people through 'the wilderness' — alerting them before the design is finished, gathering input, planning with specificity, building feedback channels, and fixing flaws in public.
points: A principal is a 'Chief Systems Officer' whose job runs on three verbs — design, implement, monitor — and the strategic plan is only the first, easiest third.

Collins and Hansen's '20 Mile March' became a literal cross-country walk: 172 school days at twenty miles a day, reported every Monday, kept the plan alive past the February point where most plans die.
The weekly cadence works as a monitoring instrument disguised as a story — the 'monitor' verb made visible in public every seven days.
Almost all school leadership is change management wearing other names: the plan does not execute itself; people execute it, so winning the people is the whole job.

Teachers are an unforgiving audience because they carry the weight of past initiatives announced with enthusiasm and abandoned without explanation; the leader's job is to walk them through 'the wilderness.'
quotes: A principal is a Chief Systems Officer. The job runs on three verbs — design, implement, monitor — and the strategic plan is only the first one.
By February, most strategic plans are already dying quietly. Not because anyone decides to abandon them. Because nobody has a weekly reason to remember what they were.
The map does not walk. The plan does not walk. The OKRs, however elegant, do not walk. People walk.
I have come to believe that almost all of school leadership is change management wearing other names.
Every new initiative arrives carrying the accumulated weight of every previous initiative that was announced with enthusiasm, executed with inconsistency, and abandoned without explanation.
The leader’s job is not to eliminate the wilderness. That is not possible. The leader’s job is to walk people through it.
